text.p: The mark ended little changed from Tuesday's close here on its Europe crosses after reversing early losses made following the U.S. election results.
Traders said the German unit has again nuzzled into small ranges and continues to gravitate about key levels against its main continental neighbours.
Any straying of the mark from 3.38 French francs, 1,000 lire or 84 pesetas of late has been limited and brief, traders said.
Despite minor day-to-day jitters the market seems to be sounding out the reference rates at which monetary union will irrevocably fix exchanges rates, analysts said.
While the firmer dollar pushed the mark lower overnight, positions were pared as two official reports on European monetary union were released later.

The European Commission released its semi-annual economic report and said EU growth will pick up next year. It said all but Italy, the U.K. and Greece would next year meet the budget deficit criteria necessary to start EMU in 1999.

Later, the European Monetary Institute, the precursor to the European central bank, said more work needed to be done to ensure sustainable fiscal consolidation after EMU. It also said ERM entry should be a prerequisite to joining EMU.

"There was very little follow-through trading after the reports, even though it is still very hard to see how the EU are going to justify allowing Italy start EMU in 1999," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.
At 1540 GMT, the mark/lira was at 1002.30/65 compared with 1002.45/95 late Tuesday. Mark/French franc was at 3.3786/89 compared with 3.3782/87 late yesterday.

The lira bounced from lows late in the day, as talk swirled that the EU monetary committee would agree to a 1,000 central ERM re-entry rate. EU Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy said the sooner the lira returns to the ERM, the better.
The mark was also capped as exaggerated fears about higher German interest rates in the months ahead were dampened this week by the latest batch of soft economic data.

The German economic recovery is fragile at best and almost completely export-led. In this environment, no one in Germany, including the Bundesbank, has any interest in seeing the mark strengthen significantly from current levels, analysts said.

"I really find it hard to see where the acceleration in German growth is going to come from at a time when the fiscal screws are being tightened both in Germany and everywhere else in Europe," said Cocks at Bank of Boston.
